artwork_title: Portrait of a lady in a black silk dress, her ruff and cuffs edged in lace
provenance: Col. That portrait bears a later inscription identifying her as Lady Emily Howard, aged 34 at the time of the portrait in 1623.  Whilst the veracity of that inscription has been questioned, it seems very likely that both portraits do indeed show a member of the Howard family, the English Heritage version having been donated by Mrs Greville Howard in 1974 and the present work having hung for many years alongside the portraits of Thomas Howard, 14th Earl of Arundel and Catherine Howard, Countess of Nottingham which currently form part of the same collection.  |  | The age given to the sitter in the present work seems questionable as she looks younger than 49.  If indeed she is Emily Howard, she was born around 1589 and was the daughter of Thomas Howard, 1st Earl of Suffolk (1561-1626) and his wife Catherine Knyvett.  She wears a costume of rich black silk brocade, open at the front to show the exquisitely fine lace of her smock or partlet showing through. She wears a ring  in the lace, and a second one is tucked into her ruff which, like her fine lawn cuffs, is edged in the same lace. A sleeveless gown is worn over her bodice and she wears a cap of black silk lace.  A mark of her high status is the fact that, pinned to her skirt, she is wearing an item of great luxury at the time - an early pocket watch.

artwork_title: Portrait of Catherine Howard, Countess of Nottingham
provenance: Col. Joseph Francis Baxendale (1877-1957) and his wife Margaret (née Heathcote, 1882-1966), Hursley Park, Hampshire | Their daughter Ruth Margaret Baxendale (1909-1989), who married Arthur Lucas (1903-1986) | Thence by descent to the present owner | | Catherine Carey (c.1550-1603) was the daughter of the 1st Baron Hunsdon who was in turn a son of Mary Boleyn, making him a cousin to Queen Elizabeth I. As a girl, Catherine entered Princess Elizabeth's household at Hatfield and through the auspices of her aunt she and her sister Philadelphia came to court as maids of honour when Elizabeth I acceded to the throne. Catherine later became a Lady in Waiting, rising to become First Lady of the Bedchamber in 1572. Elizabeth liked to have her Boleyn relatives in her inner circle and Catherine would undoubtedly have been one of the Queen's closest confidantes. She would have had a closer relationship to the Queen than most, being responsible not only for the food that was brought to her table but also presiding over the royal chamber pot. She married Charles Howard (1536-1624), Lord High Admiral of England and 1st Earl of Nottingham, under whose direction (and with significant input from Sir Francis Drake) the English fleet vanquished the Spanish Armada in 1588. Charles was a cousin of Thomas Howard, 14th Earl of Arundel, whose portrait by Gheeraerts is also presented here (lot 16). Catherine died in 1603 after a period of illness and was buried at Chelsea Old Church. The Queen was said by one contemporary source to have taken her death 'muche more heavyly' than Charles did, but they had, after all, known each other since childhood and had spent a lifetime in each other's close company. | | In the 17th Century a legend grew up involving Catherine, the Queen and the Queen's favourite Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex. Now thought to be lacking any historical basis, the story goes that the Queen gave Essex a ring that he could return to her in a time of need, whereupon she would pardon him regardless of what he might have done. In 1601 he was imprisoned in the Tower and the legend has it that he sent the ring to the Queen, but the messenger delivered it instead to Catherine. For political reasons Catherine did not pass it on and the Queen, assuming that Essex was too proud to ask for mercy, allowed his execution to proceed. This apocryphal story became the basis for Donizetti's 1837 opera Roberto Devereux. | | Robert Peake was an established court portraitist by the 1580s and he painted the Countess more than once. He has shown her here wearing a black dress with fine lace overlay; the use of black fabric was a status symbol at the time, the dye being enormously expensive to produce. Her ruff is of the finest quality linen gauze edged in lace and is supported from the back by an elaborate rebato. This device would have supported a forward-tilting ruff and in this instance was probably made from wood and wire that was wrapped in black silk thread. Wire discs covered in gossamer-thin black gauze decorate the rebato which has highlights of silver wire to catch the light; it is even possible that the round discs would have moved as Catherine walked for maximum effect. Movement was restricted by the wearing of a ruff, and the rebato would have added a further barrier to free movement, so both were indicative of high status. A full-length portrait of Catherine previously on the London art market, ascribed to Robert Peake and his studio, has been dated to around 1597, and the close similarity of the face and hairstyle suggests that the present portrait is of similar date.

artwork_title: Portrait of Thomas Howard, 14th Earl of Arundel
provenance: Col. Joseph Francis Baxendale (1877-1957) and his wife Margaret (née Heathcote, 1882-1966), Hursley Park, Hampshire  | Their daughter Ruth Margaret Baxendale (1909-1989), who married Arthur Lucas (1903-1986) | Thence by descent to the present owner |  | This hitherto unrecorded portrait by Gheeraerts of Thomas Howard was painted when the sitter was 26.  In later years he was to sit to many other great portraitists, Rubens, Mytens, van Dyck and Lievens among them, and through his patronage of art he was to become the single most influential connoisseur in England in the 17th Century.  Here we see him early in life and the reason for the commission is evident: the portrait is dated 1611, the year in which James I awarded him the Order of the Garter making him part of an elite group of only 24 knights chosen personally by the monarch.  The Howard family had had an uneasy relationship with Elizabeth I because of their Catholic faith, and their family titles had been forfeited.  These were reinstated by James I in 1604, the year that Thomas became 14th Earl of Arundel, and his elevation to Knight of the Garter some seven years later was a further endorsement by the King.  It was a great honour for any courtier, particularly one so young, and Thomas enlisted one of the most fashionable court portraitists of the day to commemorate what would have been a very significant event.   |  | Gheeraerts was the portraitist of choice at court (the favourite of James I's wife, Anne of Denmark), admired for the new sense of naturalism with which he approached his subjects. We see this in the way the young Earl's face is painted, with its subtly modulated flesh tones and the soft, wispy hair of the beard and moustache.  Gheeraerts has used Arundel's black silk costume and cloak to great effect as a foil to emphasise the colours of the gold and enamelled Garter collar.  To be portrayed in black was not only the height of fashion but was a status symbol in the 17th Century; black was the most complicated dye to make and was consequently the most expensive, so to be able to wear it denoted great wealth. But this portrait does not just capture a likeness or commemorate a significant event, it also speaks of political acceptance at the highest level.  |  | Although Arundel was a diplomat and politician, it is as a collector that he is best remembered and it is hard to overstate his importance as an art patron. Referred to by Rubens (who painted him several times) as an 'art evangelist', he had a passion for collecting that influenced not only James I and Charles I but also a generation of aristocrats and gentry who were inspired by his example to form their own collections, many of which are now the bedrock of the great country house collections of England.  In 1605 Thomas married Alethea Talbot, daughter of the 7th Earl of Shrewsbury and granddaughter of Bess of Hardwick, who inherited vast estates in Yorkshire (including Sheffield), Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire. Arundel's voracious appetite for collecting put a strain on even this considerable wealth, and by the time he died he had amassed over 700 paintings and drawings, numerous Greek and Roman marble sculptures, antiquities, coins, medals, gems, books and manuscripts, many of which are now in major institutions, in our national museums and in the Royal Library at Windsor.    Much of this collection was housed at Arundel House, the family's London seat between the Thames and the Strand, which had been taken by the Crown in the late 16th Century following Arundel's  grandfather's fall from grace and which Thomas bought back in 1607.  Among his paintings and drawings were works by Leonardo, Raphael, Parmigianino, Holbein, Dürer, van Dyck and Rubens.   |  | Arundel was one of the first British aristocrats to go on what later became known as the Grand Tour; on his voyage of 1613-14 he was accompanied by Inigo Jones, and they travelled through Europe together as far as Naples.   Jones's introduction to classical architecture, in particular the designs of Palladio, was to influence the path of British architecture for centuries to come.  With the outbreak of the Civil War Arundel, a staunch Royalist, went into self-imposed exile in Europe, settling in Padua where he died in 1646.  The Countess made her home in Amsterdam and  following her death in 1654 an inventory of the collection was drawn up which survives to give us a detailed insight into one of England's great 17th Century collections.   Arundel House was demolished in the early 1680s and the collection was sold off in 1684. |  | Marcus Gheeraerts the Younger came to England as a boy when his father, also a painter, brought his family from the Low Countries in 1568.  By 1590  the younger Gheeraerts was one of the most fashionable court portraitists in England, and in 1611, the year in which this portrait was painted, he is named by a contemporary source as 'His Mat.ies Paynter' - so he was working for the King just as he was commissioned previously by  Elizabeth I during her reign. Like many artists of the time their lives were interwoven with those of each other: Gheeraerts married John de Critz's sister Magdalena and his own sister married the miniaturist, Isaac Oliver. |  | A copy of the present portrait, listed as by 'an unknown artist', oil on canvas, 89.3 x 68 cm, was donated to Ancient House, the Museum of Thetford Life by Prince Frederick Duleep Singh (THEHM:DS.33).

He studied in London at Gray's Inn and was called to the bar in 1627. He worked for a period in Cheshire where he became Mayor of Congleton but returned to London in 1643 and became a judge at the Sherriff's Court, officiating in a number of high-profile cases that brought him into the public eye. In 1649 he was appointed Lord-President of the High Court of Justice and therefore presided over the King's trial. If the later inscription is correct this portrait shows Bradshaw at the age of 43 so would have been painted in 1645, four years before that event. | | There are few existing images of Bradshaw; a number of putative portraits of him are recorded in the Heinz Archive and Library but they all appear to show different sitters, none of whom align very closely with the image of Bradshaw in one of the few contemporary images of him, the engraving of Charles I and his Opponents which is believed to date from the 1640s (NPG D8541). The subject of the present portrait is the only contender to sport the small goatee beard of the engraved image. The National Portrait Gallery holds a pencil copy of the present work, listed as a portrait of Bradshaw, by the 19th Century copyist George Perfect Harding (NPG D5637).

provenance: Mrs F. W. Bernard | Major Stephen L. Courtauld | Mrs S. Sloan, Alexander and John Robert Cozens, The Poetry of Landscape, Yale University Press 1986, p. 158 | | In this watercolour Cozens draws our eye to the centre of the composition by the radiating diagonals of the mountains; in the foreground, goats graze and behind them, the tiny vertical form of the shrine shows in the folds of the mountains. We get a sense of the altitude and remoteness of the scene from the mist that hangs over the summit. Cozens painted two other recorded versions of this atmospheric composition, both now in permanent collections, and all three are of almost identical size: one is now in the collection of the Victoria & Albert Museum, London (3042-1876), the other is in the National Galleries of Scotland, Edinburgh (D 5023.12). For the most part the watercolours that he painted during the last decade of his life were of British landscapes, or were commissions for repetitions of Continental views first sketched during his trips to Europe in the 1770s (with Richard Payne Knight) or in the 1780s (with William Beckford). The present watercolour is unusual as it fits in to neither of these categories; he is not known to have visited Elba while in Italy and it is probably more likely that the composition was based on a drawing by his father Alexander who was there is 1746. These three versions of View on the Island of Elba were probably specific commissions, produced over a three year period between 1789 and 1792. | | Cozens's influence on Turner and Girtin is well recorded. He suffered from mental illness in his later years and was cared for by Dr Monro (1759-1833), an amateur artist and collector who was a physician at Bethlem Hospital. Monro added works by his patient Cozens to his existing collection of watercolours, his home at Adelphi Terrace doubling in the winter months as an 'academy' where young watercolourists were given encouragement and, in exchange for dinner and a few coins, were tasked with making copies of works from his collection. Among those who frequented the academy on a weekly basis were Girtin and Turner who copied many of Cozens's works, and studying his sketches of Italy became a formative part of their early training. Today Cozens is perhaps more of a cult figure than a household name, but this belies the enormous influence he had on the development of watercolour painting in Britain in the early 19th century. As Kim Sloan wrote 'John Robert Cozens had finally lifted watercolour painting out of the topographical recording of nature, to a new level where it was as capable of fulfilling the serious intentions of art as oil painting' (op. cit. p.125). | | Major Stephen Courtauld, who owned this watercolour in the early part of the 20th Century, was the younger brother of Samuel Courtauld (1876-1947), the textiles baron and renowned art collector who founded the Courtauld Institute in London. Stephen's interest in mountaineering and his love of mountain scenery was reflected in his collecting taste. He owned watercolours by many of the great early English watercolourists such as Turner, Cozens, Girtin and Cotman and in addition to the present work, he lent a number of Turner watercolours to the 1929 exhibition in Brussels.

artwork_title: The Plains of Heaven
provenance: The artist's studio | Possibly His Sale, The Contents of Lindsey House, Christie & Manson, 4 July 1854, lots 189, 190 and 191 (each being a study for The Plains of Heaven) | Jessie (1825-1859) or Isabella Martin (1812-1879), the artist's daughters | Cecilia Bonomi, daughter of Jessie Martin and Joseph Bonomi the Younger (1796-1878) and later Baroness de Cosson (1855-1944), and by descent through the family | | This watercolour is an elaborate preparatory design for John Martin's oil painting of The Plains of Heaven (Tate Britain), the most sublimely beautiful of his final three great works, his trilogy of paintings concerning The Last Judgment. Completed late in 1853, just before Martin suffered the stroke which paralysed his painting hand, this extraordinary series of enormous oil paintings was to prove a fitting swansong for this remarkable artist. Many, including some of the critics of the time, considered this series of paintings to be the pinnacle of Martin's achievements and there is no doubt that they represent a truly extraordinary high point at the very end of his life. John Martin died within only a few months of his crippling stroke, in February 1854. | | Although three preparatory sketches for The Plains of Heaven are known to have existed, only one much smaller watercolour study dated 1851 can be located today (private collection, formerly in the Campbell Collection). | | The style of sublime landscape which Martin presents in this watercolour is a form of Arcadian landscape which he had developed gradually throughout his career as an artist. It had first appeared in his painting of Clytie in 1810/11 and had been adapted for his mezzotint engravings for Milton's Paradise Lost, produced between 1824 and 1826, recurring in his oil painting of The Celestial City and River of Bliss (1841). However, this particular style of composition first crystallised in his remarkable large format watercolour of Kilmeney in 1833 and culminated in his vast oil painting of The Plains of Heaven (1851-53). | | Martin had already been developing the images which were going to form his Last Judgment subjects since the 1830s and by 1845 was producing specific pen and ink sketches for The Last Judgment itself (one in Tate Britain, formerly in the Campbell Collection). | | Martin had begun work on The Plains of Heaven, the last of his Judgment pictures, by late 1851 or early 1852 and it is recorded that he was working on this painting up to the moment that he departed for the Isle of Man where, on November 12th 1853, he was to suffer the stroke which paralysed his right hand. | | This subject was taken from Revelations chapter 21: | "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven, and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea. | And he that sat upon the throne said 'Behold, I make all things new'." | | In the finished oil painting of The Plains of Heaven Martin reversed the style of trees seen in the foreground of this preparatory watercolour design, moved the waterfall from the left to the right of the composition and introduced a host of angels, flowers and gilded gondolas to the centre of the design. Here, we see his ideal landscape in its purest form, undisturbed by the figures for which Martin was so often criticised. | | The curved upper corners which form an arched top to this watercolour correspond with the finished oil painting of The Last Judgement which was similarly shaped. The arched top is only known through Charles Mottram's engraving of the painting published shortly after Martin's death. Having ceased practising engraving himself, John Martin signed agreements with the publisher and printseller Thomas Maclean in June 1851 and January 1852, for Maclean to have the paintings engraved by a professional engraver. By January 1852 Charles Mottram had begun engraving the plate of the first painting to be finished, The Last Judgment, and Mottram's three finished plates were published together on 1st January 1857. In the engraving, The Last Judgment is seen with curved upper corners forming an arched top – this arched upper part of the painting was lost when the painting was cut into sections at some time between 1930 and 1947 (the section panels were pieced back together to form the painting now in Tate Britain). Thomas Balston was incorrect in stating that "no portion of the work was missing" (T. Balston, John Martin 1789-1854 His Life and Works, 1947, p.249), for the arched top of the painting, recorded accurately in Mottram's large engraving, was now gone. | | The handling of the present work with its rather 'staccato' style in rendering the foreground foliage, the curved up lower corners and the unresolved mountains are all typical of John Martin's later watercolour studies around 1850. He would have been unlikely to sign such an unfinished working study, especially as it remained in his possession, not exhibited to the public. Furthermore, the excellent provenance of this watercolour overcomes the lack of a signature. | | Three preparatory sketches for The Plains of Heaven were listed in the sale catalogue of the contents of John Martin's home, Lindsey House, and his remaining works, auctioned by Christie & Manson on Tuesday July 4th, 1854, lots 189, 190 and 191 in the sale. Whether this watercolour was one of those listed in the sale catalogue, or is a fourth and unrecorded study, is unknown. Indeed, it is unclear how the auction after John Martin's death was organised but it is certain that a number of the lots from the sale were either withdrawn or purchased for one of John Martin's daughters, with whose descendants they have remained until the present day. Initially they passed to either John Martin's youngest daughter Jessie Martin or, more likely, to his eldest daughter Isabella Martin. Jessie Martin had married the well known Egyptologist, Joseph Bonomi the younger (1796-1878), whilst still in her teens; however, she died in 1859, aged 34, at the birth of her eighth child. She was nursed by her elder sister, Isabella, at the end of her life and Isabella stayed to bring up the Bonomi children, assisting Joseph Bonomi in the running of the Soane Museum and in his literary work until his death in 1878. Isabella had spent her youth acting as secretary to her father, John Martin, so it was almost certainly she who safeguarded what remained. Isabella died unmarried in 1879. | | We are grateful to Michael Campbell for his assistance in preparing this catalogue note.

Wilton, The Life and Work of J.M.W.Turner, Fribourg and London, 1979, p. 481, no. 1514 where reference is made to another watercolour of the same subject, but there confused with W1512 | | Turner was to make his last journey to Switzerland in 1844; this sketch and its companion date from his penultimate trip made in the summer of the previous year, 1843, and both sheets are from a sketchbook of Whatman Turkey Mill paper dating from 1840 made by T & J Hollingworth & Co., at Turkey Mill, Boxley, near Maidstone in Kent. It stands on the Hinterrhein, a branch of the Rhine near the town of Chur in eastern Switzerland. It was approached by a wooden bridge over the dry ravine to the left, and to the right of the castle we see the spire of the 14th Century Chapel of St George. Together these ancient structures must have been an impressive sight as Turner approached them from the south, sitting as they do on a bluff rising above the river valley and at the time clearly visible from a distance of some three kilometers. Today the surrounding slopes are covered in woodland but in the 19th Century there was little to impede the dramatic view that would have presented itself to Turner as he travelled north through the Domleschg valley. | | He would probably have sketched the view from the road that winds round the contour of the hills and which we see leading into the distance on the left of the composition. Turner often made various sketches of the same subject from different viewpoints and both this and the companion study would have been drawn in pencil and coloured at a later date, either in his lodgings or back in his studio in London. At this period he often used pen and ink to outline details in his sketches but in the present works he has used the point of a brush to delineate the finer details. Elsewhere he has used short, staccato dabs of colour against broader washes, while the swirling movement of the river water is shown with large, looped strokes. | | These two sketches have an unusually interesting history, having remained together in the same family collection since the 1880s. They initially belonged to John Ruskin, the collector, writer and artist who was a lifelong champion of Turner's work. The wealth of the Ruskin family allowed him to indulge his passion for Turner's paintings and watercolours, and from 1839 onwards it is thought the Ruskins acquired more than 300 works. They lived at Denmark Hill, close to Norwood where Turner's agent, Thomas Griffith, lived; Ruskin also bought a number of works after Turner's death from Mrs Booth, the latter's housekeeper in Chelsea and Hannah Cooper, niece of Turner's stockbroker. Initially acquiring more finished works, Ruskin later started to collect sketches and was particularly drawn to the later Swiss studies; he is known to have owned several views of the Domleschg valley including the present two. | | While we do not know when Ruskin acquired them, we know that he had them with him in Venice in 1876-7 as he frequently took works by Turner with him on his travels. At the time his acquaintance John Wharlton Bunney, another English artist, was living there with his family and Ruskin commissioned him to make drawings and watercolours of architectural subjects. In the summer of 1877 Ruskin decided to return to England for a few months and left the watercolours, some books and other items in Bunney's care. In the event he suffered a mental breakdown while in England and did not return, and John Bunney himself died a few years later in 1882. His widow Elizabeth wrote to Ruskin asking what she should do with his property as she was intending to move her family back to England. Aware that she had been left in a very precarious financial situation Ruskin suggested she bring the Turner watercolours back with her and sell them to raise funds for the family, effectively bequeathing them to her. She managed to avoid parting with them and they have remained with her descendants until now. | | Sir Walter Armstrong, in his early monograph on Turner, lists an 'Alpine Valley' belonging to Michael Bunney Esq in 1902. He further, under the same listing, mentions a 'slighter sketch of the same subject (9 x 11 1/2) [which] belongs to Mrs J W Bunney'. (Armstrong, op. cit.). artwork_title: William Pitt the Younger addressing the House of Commons
provenance: Probably acquired by Count Louis Taaffe in Vienna in the 19th Century | By descent to Count Edward (Yaxi) Taaffe (1898-1967) and his Irish wife Grace McLaughlin | Sale, James H. North, Dublin, 27-28 January 1942, (lot number not recorded), £4.10 to Mrs Sylvia Hannan, and by descent to the present owner |  | This study is a preparatory work for Hickel's large scale canvas now in the collection of the National Portrait Gallery, London, donated by Francis I, Emperor of Austria in 1885 (NPG 745). There was an intended pendant to it for which a study exists showing Charles James Fox addressing the House. Pitt is shown in the old St Stephen's Chapel chamber addressing the house in 1793 in the run-up to the French Revolutionary wars. He is surrounded by nearly 100 identifiable political figures, of whom Hickel painted individual studies in preparation for the final canvas which measures 3.2 x 4.4 metres. It is currently on loan to the Palace of Westminster.
subject_matter: William Pitt the Younger, House of Commons, oil on canvas, political figures, 1793, St Stephen's Chapel, French Revolutionary wars

artist_name: Circle of Antonio Canal, called il Canaletto
artwork_title: View of the Grand Canal, looking Southeast
provenance: Most probably acquired by Max Ullmann, London, 1920s, and thence by descent to the present owner | | The present work follows Canaletto's original, Grand Canal: looking South-East from the Palazzo Vendramin-Calergi to the Palazzo Michiel dalle Colonne, now in the Birmingham Museum of Art, Alabama (gift of the Samuel H. Kress Foundation, 1961.121). | | The building with the balcony overlooking the canal, on the far left of the present view, is the 15th Century Palazzo Vendramin-Calergi. The brick structure with the battlements on the bank opposite, on the far right of the composition, is the Deposito del Megio or grain store, one of many such stores in the city. Further down the canal in the distance are the Palazzi Michiel dalle Colonne and Michiel del Brusa
